newsitem.title: UK: With candles, Dunblane remembers its dead.
newsitem.headline: With candles, Dunblane remembers its dead.

text.p: One year after a lone gunman murdered 16 first-year children in a Scottish primary school, a grieving Dunblane marks "the massacre of the innocents" on Thursday with candles, prayers and a plea to be left alone.

The shooting of the five- and six-year-olds and their teacher stunned Britain where even police on the beat carry no guns. Loner Thomas Hamilton used four handguns to mow down Gwen Mayor's Primary One class in 12 murderous minutes.
Toy guns are no longer toys in Dunblane. The gymnasium where the shooting occurred has been pulled down. Tough handgun controls are in place throughout Britain.

One year on, the school looks as ordinary as it did last March 13 when the vengeful ex-scoutmaster -- known for his keen interest in children -- burst in to take revenge on society. Hamilton took his own life minutes later.
A closely knit, sleepy town saw life turn upside down: its children killed while at play, its middle-class streets invaded by the world's media, its anonymity forever robbed.
It is still trying to pick up the pieces.
"The first anniversary is an extremely important landmark for everybody in the whole community," teacher Eileen Harrild, in the gym during Hamilton's onslaught, told BBC radio.
"We must remember the children with great dignity. But we must continue with our lives. We need to do that. I feel as a person that I need to do that now."
The school and the families of the victims have asked to be left in peace on the anniversary. Scottish police have all but commanded the media to stay away and let the relatives grieve.
"Allow them to pay their respects in private. You will appreciate that this is a very difficult and traumatic time for all concerned," Central Scotland Police said in a statement.
Prime Minister John Major planned no pronouncement, in line with the relatives' request for peace, a spokesman said.
School opened an hour late to give the children and families time to visit the site of the gym, now planted with trees.
"We'll never be the same again," headmaster Ron Taylor said. "But the school will move forward. It is a watershed on Thursday but I don't think it will be our last hurdle."

In the evening, residents will place a single candle in their front windows. Britain's best-selling daily tabloid newspaper, the Sun, urged all Britain to follow Dunblane's example as a "simple gesture of remembrance".
Harrild, who saw so much life expire, said lighted candles would show that while the children were gone, "they are still loved and there is a little piece of them in all our hearts".
Outside school, the pavements lay bare. A year ago, they were cloaked with bouquets from a stunned world. A small sign at school boundaries asked that flowers be sent to the cemetery.
Hamilton's father has wished out loud that his son were never born.
Charlie Clydesdale, whose daughter Victoria died in the massacre, said he hoped to visit the school at the hour Hamilton struck and lay down one red rose.
"Most families are trying to make it as normal a day as possible," said Karen Scott, who lost her daughter Hannah.
"The pain does not, and probably will not, go away," said her husband David. "We as a family will go to the cathedral. We may go to the cemetery."
For some, it is time to slide back into obscurity after a year of gruelling campaigning for weapon controls that ended with a controversial ban on handguns.
For others, Dunblane holds too much sadness to stay.
Barbara and Martyn Dunn moved to England after the massacre though their daughter Charlotte is buried in the town.
"She loved it here, she loved her friends, she died with her friends. So we thought we would do the right thing and leave her here," said Dunn, a mother who had once called Dunblane home.
